action_items.task: Figure out what to put on the layers and later do the design.
Review new project requirements and determine if teletext should be included.

decisions.text: Product scope changed from universal remote to TV remote control only.
Target audience confirmed as 40+ years old.
Speech recognition and LCD screens are dropped from the design.
The LED indicator will be red to show an error or low battery.
The remote control will use an intelligent chip to automatically detect and save TV patterns.
The remote control will include LEDs around buttons to light up in the dark.
The team decided to exclude speech recognition from the remote control.
The design will feature a flashy, modern look similar to mobile phones.
Buttons will light up briefly when pressed to show which button was used.
The remote control will have a single level for teletext options.

notes:
## Attendee Introductions
- Marketing Expert: Jens Damman.
- User Interface Designer: Paul Wiezer.
- Industrial Designer: Martijn Abbing.
## Project Scope and Target Audience
- Product is a TV remote control only, not a universal remote.
- Target audience is 40+ years old, specifically older people.
- Design focus is on beauty and usability for older users.
## Design Requirements and Features
- Must include good 'zap' buttons.
- Only the top 10% of buttons need to be reachable.
- Consider a home station for recharging batteries or a clap system.
- Avoid speech recognition and LCD screens due to cost and complexity.
## Design Philosophy and Aesthetics
- The product must look unique and stand out from competitors, potentially using different colors or shapes like an iMac to avoid looking cheap.
- Older users do not look for fashion or style; the main focus must be usability.
- The design should be simple, keeping in mind that elderly people do not like new features.
## Technical Functions and Buttons
- Use standard remote control methods (numbers, on/off) and large buttons with clear icons or text for elderly users.
- Include basic functions like volume, channels, on/off, and favorites, but avoid complex features like play/pause or back buttons which are too difficult for elderly people.
- Consider a 'favorite' button that sends a sequence of numbers (e.g., 666) to a specific channel, though this requires remembering the channel number.
- Implement a 'next' and 'previous' channel button, similar to a web browser, but keep it simple.
- Use a '10+' button for channels above ten, allowing users to press 1, 0, or 1, 0, 0 quickly.
- Include a mute button, though its placement is still to be determined.
## Hardware and Implementation
- The working design involves pressing a button to close a circuit, which the chip detects and sends as a pattern (like Morse code) to an LED that emits infrared light.
- The team decided to stop discussing the two-level remote control concept as it is only for television now.
## LED Indicator Design
- The LED will indicate transmission status; red is chosen for 'wrong' or low battery, green for 'okay' or active.
- The LED should be integrated into the design, possibly under or around the buttons, rather than just a separate light.
- Adding LEDs around all buttons to light up in the dark is considered a good idea for usability, similar to mobile phones.
## Chip and Pattern Logic
- The chip must produce patterns that work with all TVs; a standard chip is insufficient.
- The chip will automatically search for the correct TV pattern by turning the TV off and saving the setting.
## New Requirements and Market
- The target market is now younger than 40, so the remote should be flashy or more interesting.
- Teletext functionality is being reconsidered; the remote should primarily focus on television control.
## Design Aesthetics and Features
- The design should be flashy and popular, similar to mobile phones, prioritizing aesthetics over strict usability.
- The team considered a see-through design (like an iMac) as an option to look through the remote.
- Buttons should be simple and integrated into the design; complicated buttons are not needed.
## Lighting and Usability
- Buttons should light up briefly (e.g., 20 seconds) when pressed to indicate which button was used, similar to a telephone.
- The lighting should not be on all the time; it must activate only when the remote is used.
## Speech Recognition
- Speech recognition was discussed but ultimately rejected as not useful enough, especially given the difficulty of recognizing commands like 'TV channel one' and the need for multiple languages.
tldr: The team defined the scope as a TV remote for users over 40, focusing on usability and aesthetics while dropping speech recognition and LCD screens. Decisions included using an intelligent chip for auto-detection, adding button backlights, and creating a flashy design similar to mobile phones.
